title: Moving services offshore - Business Insurance

Moving services offshore - Business Insurance

# Moving services offshore

- by Meg Fletcher 

- Jun 18, 2006 

Some global insurers are among major financial institutions that are finding it advantageous to establish and broaden their offshore operations.

The leaders are moving beyond the offshoring of information technology programming and maintenance to embracing business process outsourcing at less costly worksites in developing countries around the world. As a result, offshore workers handle processes such as accounting, personnel management and claims for client companies that are often based in industrialized nations.

The marketplace for offshore services is targeting India now, because it has a large pool of skilled, English-speaking workers who eagerly work at globally competitive wages. The trend also is expanding to China and Brazil.

Factors that created India’s competitive work force include its language legacy from its former British colonial days, and its own far-sighted system of higher education, according to Thomas L. Friedman’s 2005 book, “The World Is Flat: A Brief History of the Twenty-first Century.” Also, the installation of fiber optic cables and other communication system improvements make the work flow possible.

evolving business

Many of India’s young workers are highly motivated to neutralize their accents and to learn about current events half a world away, so they can build rapport with the international consumers who call them seeking help or whom they call soliciting sales, said Priti Parekh, Bangalore, India-based product director for MphasiS, a global IT and BPO service provider.

There is no doubt that offshoring is a business development that will evolve and become more sophisticated, according to insurers, brokers and consultants who are involved in the process.

Offshoring is one of the 10 forces-in the form of major political events, innovations or companies-that converged to level competition around the world, according to Mr. Friedman’s analysis.

Consider the plans of London-based Aviva P.L.C. By the end of 2007, the world’s sixth-largest insurance group expects to offshore about 7,800 of its 59,000 worldwide positions, primarily to India and Sri Lanka, a company spokeswoman said.

The multiline insurer in 2002 began to send offshore portions of its “highly commoditized” home, car and travel insurance business, she said. The company adopted this strategy to meet “customers’ demands for good quality service at an increasingly low price,” she said.

While Indian workers “are particularly good at selling products,” Aviva customers are routed to call handlers close to their homes in an emergency situation-such as when an auto breaks down-because the insurer learned that customers prefer that, she said. “It’s perfectly understandable,” the spokeswoman added.

During the past three years, Aviva has broadened the range of services it has sent offshore to include IT, accounting and claims processing, she said. “Offshore operations are not an adjunct, they are an integral to our operations,” the spokeswoman said. The company emphasizes that importance through its broad program of corporate social responsibility, to which it allocates staff and resources for humanitarian projects, she said.

London-based broker Willis International Holdings has been “insourcing” several processes to its own Mumbai-based captive for more than eight years, said Jeanette Scampas, executive vp-global operations and information technology.

Willis employs about 800 people in its offshore operations and expects to expand that number “quite dramatically,” Ms. Scampas said. In addition, Willis also began sending some development work to the Philippines about six months ago, Ms. Scampas said.

The time difference is a “huge” benefit because three shifts of Indian workers give the broker 24/7 coverage, she said. “The main attraction is (wage) cost arbitrage” as well as the availability of skilled employees, she said.

Although wages for Indian IT workers are increasing at a much faster pace than in the United States, companies are still able to save a net 35% to 40% on wage costs, said Ganesh Pai, senior vp and client partner for the U.S. insurance unit of MphasiS. The company, which was begun in 1998 by Citigroup Corp. executives, now has 11,000 employees in nine countries. It has six insurer clients, he said.

worker value

Insurers learned to appreciate the value of Indian workers primarily because of their need to cope with the Y2K millennium bug issue, said Jean Gora, manager of research at the Life Office Management Assn., or LOMA, in Atlanta.

“U.S. consulting companies were afraid of the liability issue” related to Y2K work, said Suresh Gupta, head of sourcing at New York-based Capco, a global consulting firm.

Indian companies were willing to do Y2K work relatively inexpensively, because their wage costs were one-third or less than that of U.S. workers, Ms. Gora said. In addition, insurers discovered that the Indian workers “were very good,” she added.

Insurers soon began by sending IT work to India and then expanding their requests to include BPO operations, she said.

“While cost savings continue to be the dominant motivation of the transition to global sourcing models, other factors are emerging as important drivers,” including quality improvements and flexibility, according to a joint study released last month by the London Business School and Capco. The study tallied responses from 62 senior-level executives from large banking, financial services and insurance companies, including five of the top 30 insurance firms. Participants were promised anonymity, Mr. Gupta said in declining to identify them.

“These companies no longer think about ‘whether to outsource’ or ‘whether to offshore’ in terms of single functions and a single vendor; instead they are beginning to manage sophisticated sourcing frameworks that integrate multiple vendors, multiple geographies and vertical, business-specific processes,” the study found.

“The most significant management challenges in global services sourcing are often at the operational level,” the study said. “Good project management capabilities were cited as the single most important ingredient to a successful global sourcing capability.”

The number of insurers that have offshore operations is unknown, said David Snyder, vp and assistant general counsel for the Washington-based American Insurance Assn. The market for services “is highly competitive,” he said.

While offshoring insurers find they are paying less for good service, they may face challenges due to loss of control, potential loss of intellectual property as well as potential concerns about data privacy, some sources say.

backlash

In addition, a few sources say they may face an undetermined degree of backlash because of job loss in the industrial nations, such as the United States and United Kingdom, where the parent or client companies are based. Other sources, however, reject that notion or downplay it.

Among the top 10 “pain points” in alternative sourcing discussed in the survey, “negative press/social backlash” from jobs being sent offshore rated only ninth on the list.

More significant problems included the process owner’s resistance as well as a lack of cultural fit with the offshore partner, the survey found.

The survey also found that other problems, in descending order, were skepticism by top management, hidden costs, lack of performance metrics, strained relations or internal resistance to change, lack of project management skills and inadequate communications.

Despite that, “it is no longer a question of whether to outsource or offshore a generic process like IT maintenance; instead, they (companies) are already moving complex, business-specific processes offshore,” Mr. Gupta said in a statement.
